questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State the general characteristic of seed bearing plants.

(ii) How are seed bearing plants adapted to life on land? *[13 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) General characteristic of seed bearing plants** *(5 marks)*

Seed bearing plants (**spermatophytes**) are all characterised by the **production of seeds**: after fertilisation the **ovule** develops into a **seed**, a protected structure containing a young **embryo (plumule and radicle)**, a **food store** (endosperm or cotyledons) and a **protective seed coat (testa)**. Other features that go with this are:

1. They are **vascular plants** with true roots, stems and leaves, and with **xylem and phloem**.
2. The plant body is the **sporophyte (2n)**, which is the dominant generation; the **gametophyte is greatly reduced** and depends on the sporophyte (the male gametophyte is the pollen grain, the female gametophyte is the embryo sac inside the ovule).
3. They are **heterosporous**: **microspores** (become pollen grains) and **megaspores** (stay in the ovule).
4. **Pollen** carries the male gametes to the ovule, and a **pollen tube** delivers them, so **fertilisation does not need external water**.
5. There are two groups: **gymnosperms** (naked seeds, for example pine) and **angiosperms** (flowering plants, seeds enclosed in an ovary that becomes a fruit).

**(ii) Adaptations to life on land** *(8 marks)*

| Problem on land | Adaptation of seed plants |
|---|---|
| **Water loss** by evaporation | A **waxy cuticle** covers the leaves and stems. **Stomata** are mostly on the lower epidermis and are closed by guard cells when water is short. Dry-habitat plants (xerophytes) have sunken stomata, hairs, rolled leaves or thick fleshy stems. |
| **Obtaining water and mineral ions** | An extensive **root system** with **root hairs** gives a very large absorbing surface; **mycorrhizal fungi** help absorption. |
| **Transport** over long distances | **Xylem** carries water and ions up from the roots to the leaves; **phloem** carries sugars and amino acids from leaves to the rest of the plant. |
| **Support** without water to float in | **Lignified xylem vessels and fibres** (sclerenchyma), **collenchyma** in young stems, and the **turgor pressure** of cells hold stems and leaves upright. |
| **Gas exchange** in air | **Stomata** and **lenticels** (in woody stems) let $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$ pass; spongy mesophyll has **air spaces**; thin, flat leaves have a large surface for light and gases. |
| **Fertilisation** without water | **Pollen grains** have a tough outer wall (**exine**) and are carried by wind or animals; the **pollen tube** takes the male gametes to the ovule, so no swimming gametes are needed. The female gametophyte is kept **inside the ovule**, protected by the ovary. |
| **Protection and dispersal of the young plant** | The **seed** has a **testa**, a food reserve and can stay **dormant** until conditions are good; **fruits and seeds** are adapted for dispersal by wind, water, animals or explosion, so the young plants colonise new land. |

Further point: the **epidermis** protects the internal tissues from damage and from infection, and the **roots grow downwards** (positive geotropism) to anchor the plant.

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe the process of fertilization in a named flowering plant. *[7 marks]* *(5, 8, 7 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Named plant: the garden pea (*Pisum sativum*)**, a typical flowering plant (angiosperm).

**Before fertilisation: pollination.** Pollen grains, produced in the anthers, are transferred to the **stigma** (in the pea, mostly by self-pollination inside the flower). Fertilisation then takes place in these stages:

1. **Germination of the pollen grain.** The pollen grain lands on a compatible stigma, absorbs the sugary fluid secreted by the stigma and **germinates**. A **pollen tube** grows out of the grain through the wall.
2. **Growth of the pollen tube.** The tube grows **down the style** towards the ovary, guided by **chemotropism** (chemicals from the ovule), and it secretes **enzymes** that digest the style tissue to make a path. The **tube nucleus** is at the tip and controls the growth. Meanwhile the **generative nucleus** divides by **mitosis** to give **two male gametes (haploid nuclei)**.
3. **Entry into the ovule.** The tube enters the ovule through the **micropyle** and reaches the **embryo sac**. The tube nucleus **degenerates** and the tip bursts, releasing the two male gametes into the embryo sac.
4. **Double fertilisation.** The embryo sac contains the **egg cell** (with two synergids beside it), **two polar nuclei** in the central cell and three antipodal cells.
   - **One male gamete fuses with the egg nucleus** to form the **diploid zygote (2n)**, which will become the **embryo**.
   - **The other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei** to form the **triploid (3n) primary endosperm nucleus**, which will become the **endosperm** (food store).
5. **After fertilisation.** The zygote divides to form the embryo (plumule, radicle, cotyledons), the ovule becomes the **seed**, the integuments become the **testa** and the ovary wall becomes the **fruit (pod)**. The petals, stamens, style and stigma wither.

*Diagram to draw:* a longitudinal section of the carpel (stigma, style with pollen tube, ovary, ovule) and an enlarged embryo sac showing the egg, synergids, polar nuclei, antipodals and the two male nuclei entering by the micropyle.
